title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: TCC Manipulation
shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: TCC Manipulation
summary: This sub-technique covers two related macOS behaviours: abusing an already trusted application so that malicious code inherits its privacy permissions, and directly altering the Transparency, Consent and Control database. In the first case the attacker injects into a process or script that the user previously approved, so the operating system attributes the file, camera or microphone access to the trusted parent and never prompts again. In the second, when System Integrity Protection is disabled, the attacker supplies a modified database or launches a helper with crafted environment variables so the daemon loads permissions that grant full disk access to their own binary. Detection centres on the tccd service logs, which record the requesting process and the access decision, and on file integrity monitoring of the two database locations. The strongest discriminator is parentage: a permission grant whose accountable process is a shell, a scripting host or a newly written executable under a user writable path diverges sharply from the applications that normally hold those rights.

beginner.definition: macOS keeps a list of which apps may see your files, camera, microphone, or screen. Before an app gets access, the system asks you, and your answer is saved. This technique is when an attacker changes that list. They may also hide behind an app you already trusted, to gain those rights without a new prompt.
beginner.whyItMatters: These permissions are the difference between reading one file and reading everything. An attacker who gains full disk access can copy documents, messages, and saved logins. Worse, they can do it quietly, because the system believes the trusted app is still doing the asking.
howItWorks: macOS asks you to approve each app that wants protected data or devices.
Your answer is stored, so the app is not asked again for that permission.
An attacker can put code inside an approved app, which then inherits all its rights.
They may also run their own script through a signed app that already has full disk access.
If system integrity protection is off, they can alter the permission database directly.
They may point the protection service at a crafted database using start settings and variables.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk where only nurses may open the medicine cabinet. The rule is enforced by checking the badge, not the person. If a visitor borrows a nurse's badge, every cabinet opens for them and no alarm sounds. Nothing about the badge looks wrong, because it is genuine. That is what happens when harmful code runs inside an application you already approved.
takeaways: Once you approve an app, anything running inside it inherits that approval.
System integrity protection must stay on, because it guards the permission database.
Record the parent process for every permission request, not just the approved app.

objectives: Describe what the macOS privacy permission service controls and where it stores decisions.
Explain how malicious code can inherit the permissions of a trusted application.
Explain how the permission database can be modified when system integrity protection is off.
Identify the log sources and files that reveal a permission change or inheritance.
Explain why process parentage is the key evidence when reviewing a permission grant.
